title: Media and Management of Collective Psychological Crises: A Comprehensive Qualitative Analysis of Mitigation Strategies and Community Resilience Enhancement
content: This qualitative investigation examines the multifaceted role of the media in managing collective psychological crises during disasters and armed conflicts, with particular emphasis on identifying and evaluating mitigation strategies that enhance community resilience. Through semi-structured interviews with 45 purposively selected participants—media professionals, mental health experts, academic researchers, and community members directly affected by crisis media coverage, the study explores the complex, bidirectional relationship between media discourse and collective psychological responses. Interpretive phenomenological analysis was employed to capture nuanced understandings of how communities experience and interpret media narratives during traumatic events. The findings reveal that constructive journalism approaches, strategically balanced content, and institutionalized collaboration between media organizations and mental health professionals contribute to meaningful enhancements in community resilience. The study articulates the key psychological mechanisms through which media influence collective behavior and proposes an evidence-based framework—the Psychologically Informed Crisis Coverage (PICC) model—for responsible crisis reporting. The results indicate that transparent, culturally sensitive, and solution-oriented coverage can transform collective trauma responses from patterns of despair and fragmentation into opportunities for community cohesion, collective healing, and posttraumatic growth. Synthesizing emerging research on digital media effects, trauma-informed organizational practice, and culturally responsive crisis communication, the study offers actionable implications for media practitioners, organizational leaders, and policymakers seeking to align media practices with public mental health imperatives.
